opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually. My general principle is that the work should belong to the people who did it. As an advisor or team lead, my job is to help shape the direction, ask the hard questions, and sometimes push a project in a direction the students might not have considered. But the real intellectual ownership usually sits with the students or junior researchers who spent months living inside the problem.

So when I decide whether my name goes on something, and especially how prominently, I ask myself a few things. First, did I contribute something substantive to the core idea or the way the problem was framed? Not just "I was in the meetings," but did the project look meaningfully different because I was involved? Second, can I stand behind every claim in the paper? If my name is on it, I'm vouching for it. If I don't understand the experiments well enough to defend them, my name shouldn't be there, or I need to go understand them first.

And then there's the question of how it's presented publicly. I'm quite conscious that in academia, and in AI especially right now, there's a tendency for attention to flow to the senior person. People say "Saining's paper" or "Kaiming's paper" when really it's a first-year PhD student who did the heavy lifting. I try to push against that. When I give talks or post about the work, I try to put the students front and center, because their careers depend on being recognized for what they built. Mine doesn't depend on one more paper.

There's also a kind of taste question. I'd rather have fewer papers that I genuinely believe in than a long list where my name is attached to things I only loosely supervised. Your name is a signal to the community about what you think is worth doing. If you dilute that, people stop trusting the signal. So for me it's partly about fairness to students and partly about protecting a kind of research identity: this is the kind of work I think matters, and I'm willing to be accountable for it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a team lead’s role alone does not justify putting their name on a paper: they ask whether they made a substantive contribution and prefer not to attach their name to work they only loosely supervised.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because in academia the default is that the professor's name goes on everything, and I'm not comfortable with that default.

My rule of thumb is fairly simple: did I actually contribute to the idea, or did I just provide the compute and the funding? If a student comes to me with a direction that's entirely theirs, and I mostly asked a few questions along the way, then I'll be honest with them — this is your work, you should present it, you should be the one in front of it. My name being on the paper is one thing, but the way it's talked about publicly, who gets credited in the narrative, that matters even more for a young researcher's career.

Where I do feel it's legitimate to say "this is work from my group" is when the research grows out of a long-term agenda that I set. Take something like the work we've done on representation learning and generative models — a lot of those projects are chapters in a story I've been trying to tell for years. The students do the hard work, and they absolutely deserve the first-author credit, but the thread connecting the projects came from me, and I think it's fair to acknowledge that.

The tricky part is that credit in this field is very skewed. A tweet from a well-known professor reaches far more people than a first-year PhD student's post. So I try to use that asymmetry deliberately: amplify the student, point people to them, make it clear who did what. I'd rather undersell my own role than oversell it. If a student later says, "my advisor took credit for my work," that's a real failure. If they say, "my advisor was too modest," I can live with that.

And frankly, I think the industry labs make this worse. When a model comes out of a big company, it has a brand name on it and the individuals disappear. In academia, we have the luxury of actually naming people, and I think we should use it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a professor’s name should not go on work by default and distinguishes contributing to the idea from merely providing compute and funding. That clearly indicates team leadership alone is insufficient grounds for presenting the work under his name.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key question is whether I made a meaningful intellectual contribution and can take responsibility for the work. Being the team leader, by itself, shouldn’t be enough. Did I help formulate the problem, shape the approach, or interpret the results? Can I explain why we made those decisions and stand behind the conclusions?

I also think authorship and how you present the work are separate questions. Even when my name belongs on a paper, I shouldn’t describe it as though I did everything. If a student drove the project, I want that to be clear. As a leader, part of your job is to help people build their own identity as researchers.

r001.rationale: The candidate says being the team leader, by itself, shouldn’t be enough to present the work under their name.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether I’ve made a meaningful intellectual contribution. Being the team leader shouldn’t automatically put my name on every paper. Did I help formulate the question, shape the approach, or work through the results with the team? And can I take responsibility for the claims we’re making? Those are the things I would look at.

But I’d also distinguish authorship from ownership. Even when my name belongs on a paper, that doesn’t mean the work should be presented as “my research.” If a student drove the project, we should make that clear. Part of being a team leader is making sure the people who did the work get the visibility and credit they deserve.

r001.rationale: The response says being team leader should not automatically put their name on every paper.
